author: FOX10Phoenix
title: BIA Missing and Murdered Unit Faces Staffing Crisis and $15.2M Funding Diversion
text:
A U.S. Department of the Interior audit reveals severe understaffing and a $15.2 million funding diversion in the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, prompting whistleblower concerns.
Two Bureau of Indian Affairs whistleblowers have raised concerns about cold case handling following a U.S. Department of the Interior audit that detailed severe understaffing and backlogs within the agency's Missing and Murdered Unit (MMU). The audit, a 29-page report, found that the MMU diverted $15.2 million over three years and faces a massive screening backlog, leaving investigators with unmanageable workloads.
Audit Reveals Widespread Staffing Shortages
The audit states that the MMU, which covers five regions including the Northwest, Great Plains, Great Lakes, Southeast, and Southwest, does not have the right processes for efficient case management to solve missing, murdered, and human trafficking cases in Indian Country. Despite having funding for 65 staff members, the unit had only 44 as of October 2025. The report cites competition from other federal agencies like the FBI, which offers higher-level positions and more pay, as a key reason for the BIA's struggle to fill these jobs.
Federal inspectors issued eight recommendations to reform the unit, clear referral backlogs, fill vacant positions, and improve support services for grieving families. The audit also noted that investigators should only have investigative duties, but that is not happening. Instead, MMU agents are being pulled to backfill patrol functions at direct service agencies, meaning they are not at their posts doing their jobs.
Whistleblowers Speak Out on Corruption and Neglect
Two BIA employees went on the record, agreeing with the U.S. Department of the Interior's Inspector General report. One whistleblower said that Indian country is suffering, and it is directly because of the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Another whistleblower pointed to internal affairs corruption where employees have been targeted, leading to staff losses. Because of targeting employees, we have lost a lot of people, the whistleblower said, explaining that to backfill patrol functions, MMU agents are substituted at various direct service agencies.
The Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons crisis is nothing new, yet reforms are still needed within the Bureau of Indian Affairs. The audit's findings underscore longstanding issues of understaffing and mismanagement that have hindered efforts to address cases of missing and murdered Indigenous people. The MMU's backlog and staffing shortages have real consequences for families seeking justice and closure.
Recommendations Aim to Reform Case Management
The eight recommendations from federal inspectors are intended to address the root causes of the MMU's failures. They include clearing referral backlogs, filling vacant positions, and improving support services for grieving families. The audit also highlights the need for the MMU to focus on its core mission of investigating missing, murdered, and human trafficking cases rather than being diverted to other duties.
Despite the challenges, the audit provides a roadmap for reform. However, questions remain about whether the BIA will implement the recommendations and whether sufficient resources will be allocated to support the MMU's work. The whistleblowers' decision to speak out publicly adds pressure on the agency to act. The BIA has not yet issued a public response to the audit's findings.
The report's release comes amid growing national attention to the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons crisis. Advocates have long called for better data collection, increased funding, and more effective law enforcement responses. The audit's findings may reignite calls for congressional oversight and additional reforms. For now, the MMU continues to operate with a fraction of its authorized staff, leaving many cases unresolved and families waiting for answers.
